terms.comment: From sub and rapere, to snatch away from under; frequent in Plautus. The person robbed goes in the dative.

terms.register: vōx prīsca: Plaut.; old laws quoted by Cic. and Liv.
evidence: Cic. Leg. 2.22: sacrum quī clepsit rapsitve (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Rare, and mostly before Cicero (Lewis & Short); the same root as Greek κλέπτω.
Traupman lists it for “steal”: classically “to take up, carry off”, of which stealing is one use (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: tū nōn vidēris perdidisse quod petis; tē crēdō surripuisse quod pulchrē negās
phrases.english: you don’t seem to have lost what you claim; and I believe you stole what you so prettily deny

phrases.latin: Nam quī eōrum cuipiam, quī ūnā latrōcinantur, fūrātur aliquid aut ēripit, is sibi nē in latrōciniō quidem relinquit locum
phrases.english: For whoever steals or snatches something from one of the men he robs with leaves himself no place even in a band of robbers

sources: Lewis & Short: surripio · Lewis & Short: furor · Lewis & Short: clepo
